segments.narration: Physicists, computer scientists, and mathematicians all use the word vector — and they almost mean different things. But at the heart of all of it is something shockingly simple.
The simplest version: a vector is an arrow. It has two properties — how long it is, and which way it points. Change either one, and you have a different vector.

Here is the key move: slide that arrow anywhere on the page — it is still the same vector. Length unchanged, direction unchanged. The three arrows you see are identical. We pick one special home: tail at the origin.
To communicate a vector exactly, we count: how far right, how far up. Watch — three units across, then two units up, and suddenly that arrow has an address.
The first number says move this far horizontally; the second says move this far vertically. That pair of numbers IS the vector — not a location, just a recipe for displacement.
What does it mean to add two vectors? Walk the first arrow, then walk the second from where you landed. The single arrow connecting start to finish is their sum.
Now multiply a vector by a number — you just scale its length. Multiply by 2 and it doubles. Multiply by negative 1 and it flips around to point the other way.

A vector is an arrow rooted at the origin. Two numbers tell you exactly where its tip lands. Add vectors by chaining arrows, scale them by stretching or flipping — and everything else in linear algebra is built on exactly this.
